title: Dario, Daryl, and What LeBron James has got to do with Opus 5

plain_text:
It's 2018 or so. The NBA finals are starting. LeBron James just led the Cleveland Cavaliers to the NBA finals in one what is still talked about in basketball circles as the greatest individual playoff run of all time.
And here I am, in my third year of University, eating cereal in the computer lab (sue me) and watching @FTFonFS1, when the notorious (and in my eyes visionary) @getnickwright makes the most interesting remark about so-called advanced stats I've ever heard, quoting then-General Manager of the Houston Rockets, Daryl Morey (@dmorey) in the process.
For the uninitiated, advanced stats in basketball work exactly the way researchers at @deepseek_ai develop open-source models, sure, but have evals that are themselves proprietary which help them do what they do. NBA teams like the Rockets or Knicks have in-house statisticians who derive proprietary formulas for them that (try to) distill how "good" a player is into a single number. Think: PER, quarterback rating, or almost every stat in baseball at this point. You put a LOT of metrics or evals in (sports have proxies for what devs call evals), and you get one encompassing number out. Supposedly.
If that sounds familiar, it's because since the dawn of agents as we know them, and indeed before, LLM benchmarks have been trying to do that very thing well.
Sometimes they're decent. Most of the time, they aren't. 
But what do any of these things have to do with each other?
On that spring morning in 2018, probably surrounded by some hectic combination of lecture notes, computer lab goers and half-drunk cans of mountain dew, I heard Wright say, in meaning:
Daryl Morey has a rule for these "advanced stats" the math nerds come up with. If you run the numbers and they have anyone but LeBron James as the best player in the league, the stat is worthless.
What does this have to do with LLM benchmarks? Everything.
By definition, Morey's approach is unscientific. Deciding the observation then judging the merit of the experiment based on that isn't good practice by any reading of a "scientific method".
Wonder how that worked out for Morey.
Morey vs Science
"The scientific method" as a paradigm has served us admirably insofar as we do a decent job quantifying a qualitative thing.
"Size" is qualitative. "Volume" isn't. So we get to have all sorts of agreed-upon truths about size.
We did a good job on that one. It helps also that we can all agree on the formula to get there (l * w * h). More importantly, we all generally agree, for any given set of items, what makes one the biggest; no matter where you went to school, how you'd use the item, whether you happen to sell a competitor to the item, or who's paying to have the set measured and why. Not even if they're also sponsoring open source tape measure research so you can make longer ones. In anticipation of bigger items that very sponsor is likely to produce. Not that such a fantastic scenario would ever happen in the real world.
Sports performance is a little bit different than "bigness" though, isn't it? We don't yet agree on what good looks like the way we agree that 5ml is more than 2. And depending on your roster, "good" in your point guard can change meaning anyway. That makes the job of sports statisticians really hard.
IQ as a proxy for human intellect illustrates this point too. It doesn't not work. It just...doesn't quite work either. Granted, it's useful to group populations sometimes, even if not good enough to sort them (i.e. we can say "if you have 130 IQ or more you're a genius" more easily than we can defend "this 120 IQ engineer will write better code for our frontend team than that 105 IQ one"). *
Intelligence, it would seem, is tricky to resolve so finely.
 
According to this index from BenchLM, Opus 5 is the third most intelligent LLM on the planet. And that's without adjusting for price.
Is the benchmark evidence for this model's quality? Or is its quality (lack thereof) evidence against the benchmark, given the score that such a model achieved?
Every once in a while, a specimen is so clearly at or close to the extremity of a tail that we can normalize around it. Or set it as a standard and use it to check our work.
I find it the best kind of lucky that we seem to agree, all but unanimously, that Opus 5 is almost unusable. Just like Morey was lucky to be in era where it was so obvious who was the best player in the league.
To work, of course, the trick requires an excruciatingly well-qualified subjective judge. To be fair, assumptions always have. But they work terribly well.
Daryl Morey won the NBA Executive of the Year Award in 2018. The quote allegedly was uttered around 2011. Interestingly, before his assumption was essentially a foregone conclusion across his domain. He's also widely considered one of the best-drafting NBA Execs if all time.
There's something to be said for evals and benchmarking. But sometimes, you get a specimen that is so obviously good or so obviously bad that it gives you the rare privilege of having an answer key going into the benchmark test. That specimen, amusingly, becomes the benchmark to your benchmark.
A "standard", if you will.

Conclusion
Perhaps we are lucky Opus 5 is so awful.
I, for one, am a better dev for how thoroughly indifferent I've come to be about benchmarks within the top dozen models in a given class.
Plus, fitting my model, harness, and paradigm (CodeAct-ish vs ReAct-ish) combination to the task like any other part of my dev stack has been an enormous amount of fun; and a lovely return to normalcy that pays for the prep cost in time savings in the long run and vanishingly low inference costs overall.
There are a lot of models out there.  Running and/or tuning my own models fora highly scoped  scoped task me a joy I can only compare in hue to that giddy feeling I used to get when a multi-hundred-line feature  compiles for the fist time.  Due in no small part to the satisfaction of absolutely obliterating a stock model ~50x the size task-for-task. Not that I bother checking lately, to be honest.
Would recommend to one and all.
---
*this of course, assumes that intelligence is all coding requires. and that a frontend dev with more than 100 IQ can exist.
